answer: $f(x)=\dfrac1x$ (the only fixed point of $f$ is $1$, and $xf(x)$ is always a fixed point).

solutions.title: Fixed points
solutions.body:
**Injectivity and $f(1)=1$.** If $f(y_1)=f(y_2)$, then by (i) $y_1f(x)=y_2f(x)$, and $f(x)>0$ gives $y_1=y_2$. Putting $x=1$ in (i): $f(f(y))=yf(1)$; with $y=1$, $f(f(1))=f(1)$, so by injectivity $f(1)=1$.

**Fixed points.** Putting $y=x$ in (i): $f(xf(x))=xf(x)$, so $a=xf(x)$ is a fixed point of $f$ for every $x$. Let $a$ be any fixed point.

* Powers: if $f(a^n)=a^n$ then $f(a^{n+1})=f(a^n f(a))=af(a^n)=a^{n+1}$ by (i) with $x=a^n$, $y=a$. So $f(a^n)=a^n$ for all $n\ge1$.
* Reciprocal: (i) with $x=\frac1a$, $y=a$ gives $f(1)=af(\tfrac1a)$, so $f(\tfrac1a)=\tfrac1a$.

If $a>1$, then $f(a^n)=a^n\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, contradicting (ii). If $a<1$, then $\frac1a>1$ is a fixed point, again impossible. So $1$ is the only fixed point, hence $xf(x)=1$, i.e. $f(x)=\frac1x$.

**Check.** $f(xf(y))=f(x/y)=\frac yx=yf(x)$, and $\frac1x\to0$.

**Answer:** $f(x)=\dfrac1x$. ∎

prompt: Let $A$ be one of the two distinct points of intersection of two unequal coplanar circles $C_1$ and $C_2$ with centers $O_1$ and $O_2$, respectively. One of the common tangents to the circles touches $C_1$ at $P_1$ and $C_2$ at $P_2$, while the other touches $C_1$ at $Q_1$ and $C_2$ at $Q_2$. Let $M_1$ be the midpoint of $P_1Q_1$, and $M_2$ be the midpoint of $P_2Q_2$. Prove that $\angle O_1AO_2=\angle M_1AM_2$.
answer: Proof: with $S$ the external centre of similitude and $A'$ the second intersection of $SA$ with $C_1$, $SM_1\cdot SO_1=SP_1^2=SA\cdot SA'$ makes $A,A',M_1,O_1$ concyclic, and the homothety at $S$ maps $A'\mapsto A$, $O_1\mapsto O_2$, $M_1\mapsto M_2$; hence $\angle O_1AM_1=\angle O_2AM_2$.

solutions.title: External centre of similitude and a cyclic quadrilateral
solutions.body:
All angles below are **oriented angles between rays**, measured modulo $360^\circ$; equality of oriented angles gives equality of the ordinary angles.

**Setup.** The circles are unequal, so the two common tangents (which are symmetric about $O_1O_2$) meet at a point $S$ of line $O_1O_2$, the centre of the homothety $h$ with positive ratio $k=\frac{r_2}{r_1}$ mapping $C_1$ to $C_2$. Then $h(O_1)=O_2$, $h(P_1)=P_2$, $h(Q_1)=Q_2$, hence $h(M_1)=M_2$. By symmetry $P_1Q_1\perp SO_1$ at $M_1$.

**Second intersection.** Line $SA$ is not tangent to $C_1$: otherwise its image under $h$, which is the same line, would be tangent to $C_2$ at $h(A)\ne A$ while also passing through $A\in C_2$. So $SA$ meets $C_1$ again at $A'\ne A$. Since $h$ maps the line $SA$ to itself and $C_1$ to $C_2$, it maps $\{A,A'\}$ onto $C_2\cap SA$, which contains $A$; as $h(A)\ne A$ (the only fixed point of $h$ is $S$), we get $h(A')=A$.

**A cyclic quadrilateral.** In the right triangle $SP_1O_1$ (right angle at $P_1$), $M_1$ is the foot of the altitude, so $SM_1\cdot SO_1=SP_1^2$. By the power of the point $S$ with respect to $C_1$, $SP_1^2=SA\cdot SA'$. Hence
$$SM_1\cdot SO_1=SA\cdot SA',$$
with $M_1,O_1$ on one ray from $S$ and $A,A'$ on another; by the converse of the power of a point, $A,A',M_1,O_1$ are concyclic. Moreover $A$ and $A'$ lie on the same side of line $O_1M_1$ (they are on one ray from $S\in O_1M_1$, and $A\notin O_1O_2$), so the inscribed angles over the chord $O_1M_1$ are equal with the same orientation:
$$\angle(AO_1,AM_1)=\angle(A'O_1,A'M_1).$$

**Transfer by the homothety.** $h$ has positive ratio, so it maps each ray to a parallel, equally directed ray; it sends $A'\mapsto A$, $O_1\mapsto O_2$, $M_1\mapsto M_2$. Therefore
$$\angle(A'O_1,A'M_1)=\angle(AO_2,AM_2),\qquad\text{so}\qquad\angle(AO_1,AM_1)=\angle(AO_2,AM_2).$$

**Conclusion.**
$$\angle(AO_1,AO_2)=\angle(AO_1,AM_1)+\angle(AM_1,AO_2)=\angle(AO_2,AM_2)+\angle(AM_1,AO_2)=\angle(AM_1,AM_2).$$
So the oriented angles $O_1AO_2$ and $M_1AM_2$ are equal, and in particular $\angle O_1AO_2=\angle M_1AM_2$. ∎

prompt: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive integers, no two of which have a common divisor greater than $1$. Show that $2abc-ab-bc-ca$ is the largest integer which cannot be expressed in the form $xbc+yca+zab$, where $x$, $y$ and $z$ are non-negative integers.
answer: Proof: a representation would force $a\mid x+1$, $b\mid y+1$, $c\mid z+1$, giving a sum $\ge3abc$; for larger $N$ pick $x<a$, $y<b$, $z<c$ by residues and the remainder is a non-negative multiple of $abc$.

solutions.title: Residues modulo a, b, c
solutions.body:
**$2abc-ab-bc-ca$ is not representable.** Suppose $2abc-ab-bc-ca=xbc+yca+zab$ with $x,y,z\ge0$. Then
$$2abc=(x+1)bc+(y+1)ca+(z+1)ab .$$
Reducing modulo $a$: $a\mid(x+1)bc$, and $\gcd(a,bc)=1$, so $a\mid x+1$, hence $x+1\ge a$. Likewise $y+1\ge b$ and $z+1\ge c$. Then the right side is at least $abc+abc+abc=3abc>2abc$, a contradiction.

**Every larger integer is representable.** Let $N>2abc-ab-bc-ca$. Since $\gcd(bc,a)=1$, there is $x\in\{0,1,\dots,a-1\}$ with $xbc\equiv N\pmod a$; similarly choose $y\in\{0,\dots,b-1\}$ with $yca\equiv N\pmod b$ and $z\in\{0,\dots,c-1\}$ with $zab\equiv N\pmod c$. Put
$$D=N-xbc-yca-zab .$$
Modulo $a$, the terms $yca$ and $zab$ vanish, so $D\equiv N-xbc\equiv0$; similarly $b\mid D$ and $c\mid D$. As $a,b,c$ are pairwise coprime, $abc\mid D$. Moreover
$$D>2abc-ab-bc-ca-(a-1)bc-(b-1)ca-(c-1)ab=2abc-3abc=-abc .$$
A multiple of $abc$ greater than $-abc$ is $\ge0$, so $D=t\,abc$ with $t\ge0$, and
$$N=(x+ta)\,bc+y\,ca+z\,ab$$
is a representation with non-negative coefficients. ∎

prompt: Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle and $\mathcal E$ the set of all points contained in the three segments $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ (including $A$, $B$ and $C$). Determine whether, for every partition of $\mathcal E$ into two disjoint subsets, at least one of the two subsets contains the vertices of a right-angled triangle. Justify your answer.

solutions.title: Trisection points
solutions.body:
**Answer: yes.** Suppose $\mathcal E=\mathcal E_1\cup\mathcal E_2$ is a partition in which neither part contains the vertices of a right triangle.

**Three special points.** Let the side be $3$ and take $X\in AB$, $Y\in BC$, $Z\in CA$ with $AX=BY=CZ=1$. In triangle $AXZ$: $AX=1$, $AZ=2$, $\angle A=60^\circ$, so $XZ^2=1+4-2=3$ and $AX^2+XZ^2=4=AZ^2$; thus $ZX\perp AB$. By the rotational symmetry of the figure, also $XY\perp BC$ and $YZ\perp CA$.

Two of $X,Y,Z$ lie in the same part; by the rotational symmetry we may assume $X,Z\in\mathcal E_1$.

**All of $AB$ except $X$ is in $\mathcal E_2$.** For any $W\in AB$, $W\ne X$, triangle $ZXW$ has a right angle at $X$. So $W\in\mathcal E_2$.

**All of $BC\cup CA$ except $A,B$ is in $\mathcal E_1$.** Let $V\in BC\cup CA$, $V\notin AB$, and let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $V$ to $AB$ (it lies on segment $AB$). If $F\ne X$, pick any $G\in AB$ different from $F$ and $X$; then $V,F,G$ form a right triangle (right angle at $F$) with $F,G\in\mathcal E_2$, so $V\in\mathcal E_1$. If $F=X$, then $V=Z\in\mathcal E_1$ anyway (the only point of $BC\cup CA$ projecting to $X$ is $Z$, since $BC$ projects onto the half of $AB$ near $B$).

**Contradiction.** Now $Y$, $Z$, $C$ all lie in $\mathcal E_1$, and $YZ\perp CA$ with $Z\ne C$ on $CA$, so $YZC$ is a right triangle (right angle at $Z$) inside $\mathcal E_1$. This contradiction shows that for every partition, one part contains the vertices of a right triangle. ∎

prompt: Is it possible to choose $1983$ distinct positive integers, all less than or equal to $10^5$, no three of which are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression? Justify your answer.

solutions.title: Numbers with base-3 digits 0 and 1
solutions.body:
**Answer: yes.**

Let $T$ be the set of non-negative integers whose base-3 representation uses only the digits $0$ and $1$, with at most $11$ digits. Then $|T|=2^{11}=2048\ge1983$, and the largest element is $11111111111_3=\frac{3^{11}-1}{2}=88573$.

**No three-term progression in $T$.** Suppose $x,y,z\in T$ and $x+z=2y$. The number $2y$ has base-3 digits $0$ and $2$ only (doubling each digit $0$ or $1$ causes no carry). Adding $x$ and $z$ digit by digit also causes no carry, since each digit sum $x_i+z_i\le2$. By uniqueness of base-3 representation, $x_i+z_i=2y_i\in\{0,2\}$ for every digit position $i$, which forces $x_i=z_i$. So $x=z$, and there is no progression with three distinct terms.

**The choice.** Adding $1$ to every element preserves arithmetic progressions, so $\{t+1:t\in T\}$ is a set of $2048$ distinct positive integers, all at most $88574\le10^5$, with no three in arithmetic progression. Any $1983$ of them work. ∎

prompt:
Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be the lengths of the sides of a triangle. Prove that
$$a^2b(a-b)+b^2c(b-c)+c^2a(c-a)\ge0.$$
Determine when equality occurs.
answer: Equality iff $a=b=c$ (Ravi substitution turns it into $\frac{y^2}{z}+\frac{z^2}{x}+\frac{x^2}{y}\ge x+y+z$).

solutions.title: Ravi substitution and Cauchy–Schwarz
solutions.body:
**Ravi substitution.** Since $a,b,c$ are sides of a triangle, there are positive reals $x,y,z$ (the tangent lengths from the vertices to the incircle) with
$$a=y+z,\qquad b=z+x,\qquad c=x+y .$$
Expanding (a direct but routine computation),
$$a^2b(a-b)+b^2c(b-c)+c^2a(c-a)=2\left(xy^3+yz^3+zx^3-xyz(x+y+z)\right).$$

**The inequality.** Dividing by $xyz>0$, we must show
$$\frac{y^2}{z}+\frac{z^2}{x}+\frac{x^2}{y}\ge x+y+z .$$
By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Engel form),
$$\frac{y^2}{z}+\frac{z^2}{x}+\frac{x^2}{y}\ge\frac{(y+z+x)^2}{z+x+y}=x+y+z .$$

**Equality** in Cauchy–Schwarz holds iff $\frac yz=\frac zx=\frac xy$; the common value $t$ satisfies $t^3=\frac yz\cdot\frac zx\cdot\frac xy=1$, so $t=1$ and $x=y=z$, i.e. $a=b=c$.

**Answer:** the inequality holds for every triangle, with equality exactly for equilateral triangles. ∎
